title: Why do communities have traditions?
essentialQuestion: Why do people repeat certain practices over time?
learningGoal: Explain how traditions connect people and pass on knowledge, and how they can change over time.

warmUp.question: Think of any tradition, from anywhere in the world. What do people do together?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What do the people in the evidence say the meal is for?

cards.title: The yearly community meal
items: Every year, neighbours share a big meal together.
Older cooks teach one recipe to younger helpers.
This year, the organisers add vegetarian dishes.
This year, the meal also starts earlier, so more people can join.

cases.name: An elder
cases.body: “The gathering matters because we meet, teach and welcome people.”

cases.name: A young helper
cases.body: “I learned to make the bread this year. Next year I want to teach it.”

cases.name: A new neighbour
cases.body: “The earlier time means I can come for the first time.”

sections.heading: Traditions bring people together
sections.text: A tradition is a practice that people share and repeat over time. It can be a meal, a song, a game, a skill or a celebration. Many traditions mark an important time of year. Nowruz is a spring new year. Millions of people celebrate it in many countries, from south-east Europe to Central Asia. People clean, share special meals and enjoy music and dance. The community meal in the evidence is a tradition too. The elder says it matters because people meet, teach and welcome each other.
sections.simpler: A tradition is a thing people do again and again, for many years. It can be a meal, a song or a game. Many traditions mark a special time of year. Nowruz is a new year in spring. People in many lands celebrate it. They clean, share food and dance. The meal in the evidence is a tradition too. The elder says it helps people meet, teach and welcome others.

sections.heading: Traditions pass on knowledge
sections.text: Many traditions help older people pass knowledge to younger people. This is called transmission. In Korea, families and neighbours make kimchi together in late autumn. This tradition is called kimjang. They share the kimchi between homes and swap ideas. In North Africa, people learn to make couscous by watching and copying others. They eat it together at big family and community events. In Tonga, large groups perform the lakalaka. It is a dance with sung speeches about history and values. In the evidence, a young helper learns to make the bread and wants to teach it next year.
sections.simpler: Traditions help older people teach younger people. This is called transmission. In Korea, people make kimchi from vegetables. They make it in a big group in autumn. Then they share it. In North Africa, people learn to cook couscous. It is a dish of tiny grains. They watch others and copy them. In Tonga, big groups sing and dance the lakalaka. The songs tell about the past. In the evidence, a young helper learns to make bread.

sections.heading: Traditions can change and still matter
sections.text: Traditions are not frozen in the past. People adapt them to fit new times. This year, the meal adds vegetarian dishes and starts earlier, so more people can take part. The new neighbour says the earlier time means they can come for the first time. A change like this can help a tradition keep its purpose: to meet, teach and welcome. It helps when the group talks about what to keep and what to change. Not everyone in a community follows the same traditions or gives them the same meaning. No tradition is better than another.
sections.simpler: Traditions do not stay the same forever. People adapt them to fit new times. This year, the meal has food with no meat. It also starts earlier. Now a new neighbour can come. So the meal keeps its purpose. It still helps people meet and welcome others. The group can talk about what to keep. People in a group may not all do the same things. No tradition is better than another.

glossary.definition: Something a group does again and again over many years.
glossary.example: The yearly community meal is a tradition.

glossary.definition: To mark a special day or event with others.
glossary.example: Many people celebrate Nowruz in spring.

glossary.definition: Passing knowledge or skills from one person to another.
glossary.example: Teaching the bread recipe to a young helper is transmission.

glossary.definition: To change something so it fits a new need.
glossary.example: The organisers adapt the meal by adding vegetarian dishes.

glossary.definition: The reason why something is done.
glossary.example: The purpose of the meal is to meet, teach and welcome people.

checks.question: What is one purpose of the community meal?

options.text: To prove that everyone eats the same food
options.feedback: Not quite. The meal shares a recipe. It does not prove what everyone eats. Look at what the elder says.

options.text: To stop the tradition from ever changing
options.feedback: Not quite. The meal changed this year, so it does not stop change. Look at what the elder says.

options.text: To teach a recipe to younger people
options.feedback: Yes. Older cooks teach one recipe to younger helpers. The elder says the meal is for meeting, teaching and welcoming.

checks.question: What does the change to an earlier time show?

options.text: The tradition has now come to an end for all.
options.feedback: Not quite. The meal still happens every year. Look at what the new neighbour says.

options.text: The group wants more people to take part.
options.feedback: Yes. The earlier time means a new neighbour can come for the first time.

options.text: Traditions can never change in any way.
options.feedback: Not quite. The time did change, so traditions can change. Look at what the new neighbour says.

checks.question: Before the group changes the meal again, what should they ask people?
checks.placeholder: Think about what matters most to the people who come, and who might be left out ...

write.prompt: Do the changes help the meal keep its purpose? Use the elder's words and one other detail from the evidence.
sentenceStarters: The purpose of the meal is ...
selfCheck: I named the purpose of the meal.
I used the elder's words and one other detail.
I did not call any tradition better or worse.
write.example: The purpose of the meal is to meet, teach and welcome people. The elder says this is why the gathering matters. One change is that the meal now starts earlier. This could help because a new neighbour can come for the first time. The vegetarian dishes may also let more people eat together. So the changes can help the meal keep its purpose. The organisers should also ask people which parts matter most to them.

speak.partnerTask: Explain one reason people keep a tradition. Your partner explains one reason a tradition might change.
speak.independentTask: Describe a tradition you know, or one from the lesson. Say what it teaches younger people.

watch.title: Why Is It Important to Share Culture?
watch.why: People at a festival of living traditions explain why sharing culture matters.
watch.beforeQuestion: Why might people want to share their traditions with others?
watch.afterQuestion: What does respectful sharing of a tradition look like?
watch.summary: This video was made at the Smithsonian Folklife Festival in Washington, D.C., in the United States. The festival invites people from many communities. They share their music, dance, crafts and food. In the video, people at the festival talk about why sharing culture matters. Sharing culture helps people learn about each other. It helps them see the world in new ways. It can help people stay strong in hard times and feel joy in good times. Each speaker gives their own view. No one person speaks for a whole culture. When you share with respect, you listen to the people who practise a tradition. You also give them credit.
keyPoints: Sharing culture helps people learn about each other.
Each speaker shares their own view, not the view of a whole culture.
Respectful sharing means listening and giving credit.

reflect.completionMessage: You finished Lesson 17. You explained how traditions connect people and how they can change over time.

visual.description: The community meal from the evidence: a long outdoor table in late-afternoon light. An older cook shows a young helper how to shape bread, a new neighbour is arriving and being welcomed, and a hand-written sign says “Now starting earlier – vegetarian dishes today”. In three small circles around the edge: people making kimchi together, a large shared dish of couscous, and a row of lakalaka dancers.
visual.alt: Neighbours share a meal at a long table while an older cook teaches a young helper to make bread. Small pictures show kimchi making, a dish of couscous and Tongan dancers.

educatorNotes: Learners may know some of these traditions well, and may practise them differently from how the lesson describes them. Treat their knowledge as expert knowledge, but never ask anyone to explain their own family's or community's traditions.
Some learners may be far from people they used to celebrate with, so traditions can bring mixed feelings. Keep the focus on the fictional meal and the lesson examples, and let sharing be optional.
You could swap in a tradition from your local area, such as a harvest festival or a shared community meal, if someone who takes part can describe it.
changes: Expanded the reading from about 80 to about 290 words, with real traditions from several regions: Nowruz (south-east Europe to Central Asia), kimjang (Korea), couscous (North Africa) and lakalaka (Tonga).
Expanded the fictional community meal with two new voices (a young helper and a new neighbour) so learners have evidence for both transmission and change.
Rewrote simpler English at a much lower level and added a third section on how traditions change.
Added a warm-up, self-check and visual plan; fixed glossary words that never appeared in the text.
Moved correct answers out of the first position and rewrote feedback to point back to the evidence.
Replaced the general UNESCO page and the video link in sources with pages that back up the new facts; removed the next-lesson field.
